data.text/markdown:
think vs. know in CHILDES

The syntactic-only hypothesis: a verb that occurs with both declarative and interrogative complements is veridical (responsive); one that occurs with only one is not. This notebook measures that input for think and know in Eng-NA + Eng-UK (childes-db 2026.1 on Redivis), and checks that every benchmark word is frequent enough for a CHILDES-trained model to learn.

Vocabulary frequency

A multiword entry ||(p||) gets its whole-word phrase count, and ||(\min_{w \in p} \mathrm{count}(w)||). An entry is below threshold when that minimum is under 10: some word in it is too rare to learn. Templates like <person>'s are skipped.

data.text/markdown:
vocabulary.csv keeps two frequency columns, for thresholding its entries later:
  • childes_count: ||(\mathrm{count}(w)||), or the whole-word phrase count for a multiword entry.
  • childes_lemma_count: ||(\mathrm{count}(\ell)||), the number of CHILDES morphemes (token_morpheme, stems and clitics alike) with lemma ||(\ell||), where a word's ||(\ell||) is the lemma CHILDES most often gives its stem morpheme (papers → paper, hid → hide, message's → message). A contraction unattested as a gloss (meeting's) takes its base word's lemma; any other unattested word counts 0. A multiword entry gets its rarest word's lemma count, ||(\min_{w \in p} \mathrm{count}(\mathrm{lemma}(w))||). Templates like <person>'s stay blank.

data.text/markdown:
Alternatives for rare words

Each word's tag is its most frequent CHILDES %mor tag: part of speech plus word-level features (noun-Plur, verb-Fin Past), so a replacement keeps number, tense and gender. Case, subject agreement and mood vary with the utterance, so they are dropped. An unattested word takes the tag of its nearest attested neighbour. Candidates are words with that tag and ||(\mathrm{count} \ge 10||), ranked by cosine similarity of spaCy en_core_web_lg vectors (md shares 20k vectors across its whole vocabulary, so rare words get their neighbours' vectors): ||(\cos(v_w, v_c) = v_w \cdot v_c / (\lVert v_w \rVert \lVert v_c \rVert)||). Similarity ranks plausible swaps; the requires features in vocabulary.csv (breakable, liquid, ...) still need a manual check.

data.text/markdown:
Complement classification

Each think/know token tagged verb on the CHILDES %mor tier is classified from its CHILDES %gra dependency parse (UD relations; utterances with any unparsed token are skipped). UD attaches a PP's noun as obl with the preposition as its case dependent, and keeps n't on its auxiliary (don't is one token). Only dependents whose whole span is right of the verb count as complements, checked in this order:
  • interrogative: a clausal dependent (ccomp/xcomp/advcl) whose first word is whether, if, or a wh-word; or a wh-word object (you know what?, wh_bare; I know what you mean, wh_object, where free relatives and concealed questions are indistinguishable).
  • declarative: a ccomp otherwise (that if it starts with complementizer that, else zero). A clause whose first if/wh-word sits in an adverbial or subject clause inside it is declarative too (adjunct_first: I think [if you push it] it'll go, I think [what we'll do] is play).
  • infinitival (think to), so (think so), NP (object), PP (about/of).
  • With nothing to the right: matrix_wh (what do you think?), left_clause (parentheticals, it's raining I think), else none (I don't know).
Cross-check: spaCy (en_core_web_md) runs the same rules on its own parse of each utterance. CHILDES glosses have no punctuation, so its input ends in ? for question-type utterances and . otherwise, and i is capitalized. Its known-answer check uses the benchmark's think/know single sentences, which carry embedded_type labels with the same names and have no CHILDES parse. Benchmark none includes parentheticals, which the rules split into left_clause by design.

data.text/markdown:
Verb frequency

The 50 most frequent verbs across all speakers, counting each %mor verb token toward its stem (knows, knew → know). Auxiliaries and copulas carry their own tags, so they're excluded.

Is the contrast categorical?

The hypothesis reads "occurs with both" categorically, so a handful of genuine think + interrogative tokens would count. Utterances within a transcript are correlated, so the 95% CI on ||(p = n_\text{interrog} / (n_\text{decl} + n_\text{interrog})||) comes from resampling transcripts with replacement (2000 draws). Below that: how many corpora have any think + interrogative token, and a sample of such tokens with the turn before and after (speaker codes as in the transcript, the token's own turn in brackets), for checking by hand whether they are parse errors.

Ablation sweep

Let ||(I_k||), ||(D_k||), ||(N_k||) be know's interrogative, declarative and total counts, and ||(I_t||), ||(D_t||) think's. Removing a fraction ||(f||) of know + interrogative uses leaves know with ratio ||(D_k / ((1-f) I_k)||) and removes a share ||(f I_k / N_k||) of all know uses (the confound). Counterfactual 1 relabels those ||(f I_k||) uses as think, giving think the ratio ||(D_t / (I_t + f I_k)||). Figure criterion. If the input supports the syntactic hypothesis, know's ratio at ||(f = 0||) sits well below think's (know takes far more interrogatives), and the two curves cross for some ||(f||). The right panel tests the planning claim that full ablation removes over half of know's uses: it holds if the curve ends above 0.5 at ||(f = 1||). Augmentation (counterfactual 2, bottom row). Add ||(m I_k||) think + interrogative uses and leave know as observed. Think's ratio becomes ||(D_t / (I_t + m I_k)||), and the added uses are a share ||(m I_k / (N_t + m I_k)||) of all think uses (the confound: synthetic think input). Think's ratio falls to know's observed ||(D_k / I_k||) at ||(m^* = (D_t I_k / D_k - I_t) / I_k||). The criterion: the think curve crosses know's line at ||(m^*||). The right panel shows how much of think's input that takes.
